title: Iron Leaf Robotics — Ground-Sensing Cart for Orchards & Vineyards
summary: A human-pushed sensing cart that records geolocated camera, lidar and IMU data along every row, turned into human-checked grower reports of gopher activity and irrigation stakes. Demoed on five Okanagan farms in fall 2026.

heroVideo.alt: Ryan pushing the sensing cart down an orchard row in fall colours

overview: I founded Iron Leaf Robotics in 2026 to give orchard and vineyard growers row-by-row field data. Growers walk or drive their rows to find problems, and gophers in particular are hard to get ahead of on foot. The first product is a human-pushed sensing cart that records every row, and a report of gopher activity and irrigation stakes that look out of line, where every mark is one I confirmed by eye.

The cart is deliberately a learning vehicle: pushing by hand lets me iterate on sensing, calibration and data quality before spending on autonomy. Grower interviews started in May 2026, the cart's first field run was Sept 30, and I went full-time on Oct 20 to run weekday demos before the leaves fell.
objectives: Record every row with timestamped, geolocated imagery that future models can be re-run against.
Turn a field visit into a report a grower can act on, with each mark confirmed by a person.
Learn from growers which jobs are worth automating before building a powered robot.
Build a labelled dataset fast enough to train detection models alongside the hardware.
role: Founder: customer discovery, grower interviews, demos and pilot letters of intent
Electrical, controls and mechanical design of the cart
Cart software, data pipeline and report tooling, written with AI coding tools (Codex and Claude Code)
Data labelling and prototype computer-vision models
process: Interviewed eight growers from May to October 2026, before and alongside the demos; seven of the eight said they want gopher control.
Kept the cart human-pushed so sensing and calibration could be iterated in the field without adding propulsion as another failure source.
Between demos I tilted the lidar down 15° for a 2.5D ground scan and added stereoscopic Ethernet (PoE) cameras, which have now recorded on three farms.
A frame-ranking model sorts the footage for my review; every mark in a grower's report is one I confirmed by eye.
results: The first five field runs (Sept 30 to Oct 17) totalled about 181 minutes, about 6.2 km of distance driven and about 171,000 camera frames, with 0 raw-file checksum failures.
Demos have run on five farms this fall; anonymized sample reports are public at ironleafrobotics.ca/sample-report.

First model: a frame ranker trained on 546 frames I reviewed ranks gopher-mound frames above chance on farms it never trained on (30 of 30 held-out runs). It is used internally to speed up review, not as a detector.
About 5,000 mound frames and 3,000 irrigation-stake frames labelled so far.
One grower has signed a non-binding letter of intent for a 2027 pilot.
Next: detection models that hold up on farms they haven't seen. Prototype model output shown here is not validated.

title: UBCO Aerospace — 2026 Urban Firefighting Drone System
summary: Electrical-system leadership for a multi-drone autonomous firefighting project that won the 2026 AEAC Innovation Award.
overview: From January 2025 to June 2026, I served as Director of Electrical for the UBCO Aerospace Team across two AEAC competition seasons.

The team finished 9th overall in 2025. For the 2026 urban-firefighting mission, the rules did not require multiple aircraft, but we deliberately chose a mothership architecture instead of the more conventional single-aircraft approach. That architectural decision became the defining innovation of the 2026 system and was recognized with the AEAC Innovation Award.
objectives: Create an electrical system that could support the team's mothership concept without making integration fragile.
Give autonomy and sensing teams dependable power, data interfaces, and fault boundaries.
Reduce electrical mass and integration risk while keeping the aircraft practical to assemble, test, and troubleshoot.
Make cross-team interfaces explicit enough that electrical, mechanical, autonomy, and software work could progress in parallel.
role: Directed the electrical subteam and owned the top-level electrical architecture.
Defined electrical interfaces with autonomy, software, sensing, communications, and mechanical subsystems.
Led design reviews, work breakdown, milestone planning, and integration readiness.
Designed and integrated key power-distribution, sensing, and communications hardware.
process: Mapped power, data, sensing, and communications interfaces around the mothership concept before committing to detailed hardware.
Integrated LiDAR, RTK GNSS, IMU, cameras, LTE, Ethernet, and CAN around the flight/autonomy compute.
Designed the protected distribution architecture and a custom 50 V to 5 V, 40 W synchronous converter that reached approximately 92% efficiency.
Used peer review, milestone gates, and subsystem readiness checks to reduce late electrical/software/mechanical conflicts.
results: The mothership architecture received the 2026 AEAC Innovation Award.
The competition aircraft integrated the required sensing, communications, power, and autonomy hardware into a working system.
The custom 50 V to 5 V, 40 W synchronous converter reached approximately 92% efficiency.

title: Mountain Resort Data Collection System — UBC Capstone
summary: A low-power distributed sensing system using ESP32 edge nodes, LoRa networking, ToF/mmWave sensing, custom power electronics, and a Linux gateway.
overview: My UBC capstone team developed a low-cost distributed sensing system for mountain-resort deployment. The project combined anonymous skier-flow sensing, localized environmental data collection, long-range wireless networking, battery-powered edge nodes, and a centralized gateway/dashboard architecture.

The deployment problem was inherently geographic: sensing points were spread across a large mountain with limited power and network infrastructure. The conceptual-design work used Big White as the reference environment, including gateway-coverage studies, seasonal battery constraints, cold-weather operation, and Canadian 915 MHz wireless requirements.
objectives: Track skier movement anonymously so resorts could understand flow and occupancy without collecting personally identifying information.
Collect localized weather/environmental measurements from distributed points across the mountain.
Operate remote nodes through harsh seasonal conditions with battery replacement intervals practical for resort staff.
Maintain long-range communication across variable terrain while avoiding dependence on external network coverage.
Demonstrate the complete path from field sensing through the gateway to database/dashboard visualization.
role: Owned the node electrical design from battery assumptions through PCB implementation.
Designed the custom PCB schematic/layout and supported assembly and bench validation.
Selected batteries and electrical components against the deployment constraints.
Researched LoRa and sensing options and documented the resulting design decisions.
process: Used distributed nodes to support both anonymous skier-flow sensing and localized weather measurements across the resort.
Used ESP32 edge nodes and a Linux gateway so low-power sensing could remain distributed while storage and visualization stayed centralized.
Implemented power conversion, battery monitoring, and low-voltage protection on the custom node hardware.
Bench-tested the electronics, then validated LoRa communication and the complete sensor-to-dashboard data path.
results: Demonstrated more than 500 m outdoor LoRa communication.
Demonstrated end-to-end sensing-to-dashboard data flow.
Completed custom PCB schematic, layout, assembly, and bench testing.

title: “Chimera” FPV Drone Frame
summary: A crash-driven custom FPV frame redesign focused on center-of-mass placement, crash behavior, packaging, and lightweight manufacture.
overview: The project started with an off-the-shelf 5-inch FPV frame, not a clean-sheet custom design. Two major crashes exposed different weaknesses and drove two separate engineering responses.

The first failure followed a failed dive: an arm tore off and the motor wiring pulled hard enough on the electronics to rip copper traces from the ESC. Rather than adding a heavy bracket or strain-relief assembly, I rerouted the motor wires around a flight-controller standoff so crash loads were reacted mechanically before reaching the PCB.

A second major crash broke an arm again. By then I also wanted to carry a GoPro Session 5. That combination drove the full frame redesign: raise the arms around the central body, improve component protection and packaging, and create a geometry better suited to protecting the camera during impacts.
objectives: Prevent arm-separation loads from being transferred directly into ESC/PCB traces.
Keep the first wiring fix extremely light and simple enough for an FPV aircraft.
Redesign the frame after the second critical crash rather than continuing to repair the off-the-shelf architecture.
Protect a GoPro Session 5 by bringing the arms upward around the central package.
Improve component packaging, center of mass, footprint, repairability, and crash behavior before manufacturing the final carbon-fiber/aluminum version.
role: Diagnosed crash-load paths from two critical failures of the original off-the-shelf frame.
Developed the standoff-based motor-wire strain-relief routing after the first crash.
Owned the custom SolidWorks frame geometry and GoPro Session 5 packaging concept after the second crash.
Ran printed fit/prototype iterations before final carbon-fiber/aluminum manufacture.
Integrated and validated the electronics in the revised frame.
process: Failed dive → arm separation → motor-wire tension → ESC copper traces damaged.
Wrapped/routed the motor wires around a flight-controller standoff so impact tension was reacted mechanically before reaching the PCB.
A later critical crash broke an arm again; recurring arm failure plus the desire to carry a GoPro Session 5 justified a full frame redesign.
Raised the arms around the central package, revised battery/electronics packaging, and iterated the geometry using printed prototypes before final manufacture.
results: The first crash produced a lightweight wiring/strain-relief solution that reduced direct PCB loading from motor-wire tension.
The second crash triggered a full custom-frame redesign instead of another off-the-shelf repair.
The final frame incorporated raised-arm geometry, revised component packaging, and GoPro Session 5 protection into carbon-fiber/aluminum hardware.

decisions.decision: Route motor wires around a flight-controller standoff
decisions.why: The first crash tore an arm away and the attached motor wires transferred the load into the ESC hard enough to rip PCB traces.
decisions.tradeoff: The routing had to provide useful strain relief without adding a bulky guard, bracket, or meaningful mass.
decisions.evidence: The revised routing created a mechanical load path around the standoff so the PCB was no longer the first structure reacting motor-wire tension.

decisions.decision: Stop repairing the off-the-shelf frame and redesign the architecture
decisions.why: A second critical crash broke another arm, showing that the recurring structural failure was worth addressing at the frame level rather than through repeated replacement.
decisions.tradeoff: A clean-sheet frame required CAD, prototyping, electronics repackaging, and final-part manufacture instead of simply buying another arm.
decisions.evidence: The redesign progressed through printed prototypes into final carbon-fiber/aluminum components.

decisions.decision: Raise the arms around the center package
decisions.why: The new frame also needed to carry and better protect a GoPro Session 5 during impacts.
decisions.tradeoff: Arm elevation changed packaging, geometry, structural load paths, and component clearances and therefore had to be validated as a complete system.
decisions.evidence: The raised-arm concept became a defining feature of the final custom frame geometry.

iteration.observed: Crash 1 showed that a broken arm could destroy electronics through the motor-wire load path; Crash 2 showed the off-the-shelf frame itself had become the recurring limitation.
iteration.changed: First, the wiring path was strain-relieved around a flight-controller standoff. Later, the frame architecture was redesigned with raised arms, revised packaging, and GoPro Session 5 protection as explicit requirements.
iteration.verified: The custom design moved through CAD and printed prototypes into final carbon-fiber/aluminum hardware and subsequent flight/crash use.

projectSummary: A custom FPV frame redesign driven by two critical crash failures on an off-the-shelf frame: first to eliminate ESC/PCB stress with almost no weight penalty, then to protect a GoPro Session 5 and improve crash behavior through a new raised-arm architecture.

title: Axial Flux Brushless DC Motor
summary: A custom axial-flux BLDC motor and geared scissor mechanism built with custom coils, 3D-printed structure, and iterative troubleshooting.
overview: This university project developed a custom axial-flux BLDC motor and geared scissor-cutting mechanism using 3D-printed mechanical parts, custom-wound coils, and existing drone hardware.

The axial configuration was chosen instead of defaulting to a conventional radial layout. Its layered construction made the motor easier to reason about as separate rotor, air-gap, stator/coil, and structural interfaces, so parallel iterations could be made without forcing a complete redesign every time one layer changed.
objectives: Demonstrate a functional custom motor rather than optimize a textbook geometry.
Use the axial layout to keep rotor, winding, air-gap, and structure changes as independent as practical.
Prove the motor against a real mechanical load and use failure as design feedback.
role: Team captain and motor-architecture lead
Mechanical/CAD design of the motor assembly
Coil geometry, winding, and electrical integration
Prototype fabrication and test troubleshooting
process: Selected an axial-flux configuration so rotor, coil/stator, spacing, and structure could be iterated as distinct layers around stable interfaces.
Designed six coils in a wye configuration while balancing magnetic air gap, structural rigidity, packaging, and manufacturability.
3D printed the structure, wound and wired the coils, assembled the motor, and integrated the geared scissor mechanism.
The motor ran under mechanical load; PLA thermal deformation and rotor stability exposed the main limits of the first structural implementation.
results: The custom axial-flux motor ran and drove the geared scissor mechanism.
Load testing exposed PLA thermal deformation and rotor-stability limits that define the next structural revision.
evidence: Show the motor doing mechanical work.
Turn the V1 limitation into an iteration story.
